questions.prompt: Estimate ΔH for H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g). Average bond enthalpies are H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, and H–Cl 431 kJ/mol of bonds. Use energy required for bonds broken minus energy released forming bonds.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Break one H–H and one Cl–Cl, costing 436 + 243 = 679 kJ; form two H–Cl, releasing 862 kJ. The estimate is 679 − 862 = −183 kJ. A reverses subtraction. B counts only one H–Cl product bond. D assigns the breaking-energy total a release sign and ignores product formation.

questions.prompt: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), use N≡N 945, H–H 436, and N–H 391 kJ/mol of bonds. What ΔH is estimated for the equation as written?
questions.explanation: D is correct. Breaking costs 945 + 3(436) = 2253 kJ. Two ammonia molecules contain six N–H bonds, forming which releases 6(391) = 2346 kJ. Difference is −93 kJ. A reverses the sign. B omits N2 bond breaking. C counts only two N–H bonds, one per ammonia, instead of three per molecule.

questions.prompt: For gas-phase CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, use C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 328, and H–Cl 431 kJ/mol of bonds. Three C–H bonds occur unchanged on both sides. What is the estimated ΔH?
questions.explanation: A is correct. After canceling unchanged bond counts, break one C–H and one Cl–Cl and form one C–Cl and one H–Cl: 413 + 243 − 328 − 431 = −103 kJ. B reverses the subtraction. C omits H–Cl formation. D subtracts the three retained C–H bonds without also including their corresponding reactant contribution. Cancellation is accounting, not a claimed elementary mechanism.

questions.prompt: Estimate ΔH for C2H4(g) + H2(g) → C2H6(g). Use C=C 614, C–C 347, C–H 413, and H–H 436 kJ/mol of bonds. The four original C–H bonds cancel in the net inventory.
questions.explanation: B is correct. The remaining accounting is 614 + 436 − 347 − 2(413) = −123 kJ. A reverses the sign. C omits the two additional product C–H bonds. D omits the reactant C=C breaking contribution while retaining the product bond terms. Replacing a double bond by a single bond must account for both complete bond enthalpy values.

questions.prompt: For 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g), a bond-energy model gives ΔH = −484 kJ. Using H–H 436 and O=O 498 kJ/mol, what average O–H bond enthalpy makes the model consistent?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Broken-bond cost is 2(436) + 498 = 1370 kJ. Let D be O–H enthalpy; four product bonds give −484 = 1370 − 4D, hence D = 463.5 ≈ 464 kJ/mol. A ignores the reaction energy. B uses its sign incorrectly. D divides the formation-energy total by two water molecules rather than four O–H bonds.

questions.prompt: Which bond-energy account is consistent with an exothermic chemical reaction?
options: Energy released by forming product bonds exceeds energy required to break reactant bonds.
Breaking reactant bonds releases the energy, while forming product bonds always absorbs it.
Every individual bond change must release energy, so no reactant bond can be broken.
The total breaking cost must equal formation release in every balanced reaction.
questions.explanation: A is correct. A negative broken-minus-formed result means formation releases more than breaking requires. B reverses the energetic roles of breaking and forming. C confuses net release with the sign of each contribution. D mistakes atom conservation for equality of bond-energy totals; bonds and molecular environments can change even though atoms are conserved.

questions.prompt: Why is a reaction enthalpy calculated from tabulated average gas-phase bond enthalpies usually an estimate rather than an exact value for a particular molecular reaction?
options: Energy conservation does not apply to gas-phase reactions.
Every bond with the same element labels has exactly the same enthalpy in every molecule.
Average tables include only product bonds and cannot describe breaking.
The actual bond energies depend on molecular environment, while the table averages related bonds across environments.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Molecular surroundings affect bond strengths, so averages need not reproduce every specific reaction exactly. A incorrectly removes conservation. B states the opposite of the environment dependence. C misrepresents the same positive bond-breaking values, which can be used with opposite signs for formation. Phase effects may also require separate accounting if nongaseous species are requested.

questions.prompt: A gas-phase bond estimate for 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O(g) is −484 kJ. At the same specified reference conditions, each mole H2O(g) → H2O(l) has ΔH = −44.0 kJ. What estimate follows when the reaction product is two moles liquid water instead?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Add condensation of both water moles: −484 + 2(−44.0) = −572 kJ. A ignores the phase contribution. C assigns condensation the vaporization sign. D accounts for only one mole. Gas-phase bond inventories alone do not include the energy change associated with forming liquid-phase intermolecular contacts.

questions.prompt: The gas-phase bond dissociation Br2(g) → 2Br(g) requires 193 kJ per mole Br2. What heat corresponds to dissociating 0.200 mol Br2 under the specified bond-energy model?
questions.explanation: D is correct. One Br–Br bond is broken per Br2, so q = 0.200(193) = +38.6 kJ. A gives the sign for recombination. B uses a one-mole amount. C divides by amount instead of multiplying. Producing two atoms does not mean two initial Br–Br bonds were broken per molecule.

questions.prompt: One bond requires 450 kJ/mol to break and another requires 300 kJ/mol. Without a complete reactant/product bond inventory, which conclusion is justified?
options: A reaction involving the 450 kJ/mol bond must always be more exothermic.
Forming the 450 kJ/mol bond must absorb more energy than forming the 300 kJ/mol bond.
Breaking the first bond requires more energy per mole, but a full reaction enthalpy also depends on the other bonds broken and formed.
Both require equal energy because each is described as one bond.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The dissociation comparison is direct, but a net reaction includes the complete energy balance. A infers an overall sign from only one breaking contribution. B incorrectly treats bond formation as endothermic in this model. D ignores the given different bond enthalpies. Stronger individual bonding does not by itself specify a whole reaction's energy change.

questions.prompt: Estimate ΔH for CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g). Use C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O in CO2 799, and O–H 463 kJ/mol of bonds.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Break four C–H and two O=O: 2648 kJ. Form two C=O and four O–H: 3450 kJ. Difference is −802 kJ. A reverses the subtraction. C counts only one C=O in CO2. D counts only one O2 bond instead of two. Product water is explicitly gaseous, so no condensation correction is included here.
